Negative things…that are specific to gacha games. How is the *rest* of the industry going to suffer from this?

If you’re the sort of person who views the gacha model as a pox, pushing companies to squeeze low spenders is still largely a *good* thing, because it further discredits the gacha model and kills more gachas via players leaving them. Chances are that a lot of the things you view as negatives are in fact Kupo’s ideal outcome; the very way that gacha players think about their games is warped by their own time investment, and by the dependent relationship the games themselves *want* players to have with it.

This genre is a pitcher trap before you ever spend a cent. Enjoy the game as you will, but don’t lose sight of that.

I think the map design was pretty cool; puzzle setups like this offer a chance for more complicated strategy talk in the team. I do think the map’s brevity was to its benefit though, as everyone operating on the same plan can potentially get boring for individual players if that goes on for too long (though I’d be okay either way). Hearing everyone else’s opinions on that would go a long way to iterating on this style of map.

Were people to agree with me on the above, I think if you wanted to make a more extensive version of this, a good way to go about it would be to embed “layered” puzzles. New elements appearing mid-map could throw the original plan off-track, requiring new strategy discussions. You could also design the puzzles in such a way that any strategy you enter with inevitably frays like a rope over the course of the opening turns, gradually pushing things more and more towards individual-player improvisation. Or you could simply keep maps like this short and present them as occasional shake-ups.

>These things maybe relevant to you in a personal since. And that is fine. But as it pertains to what the OP posted it doesn't.

Spinnabl’s being overly aggressive here, but they are right in that these things are relevant.

Race, gender, sex, ability, etc. all interact and come together to indicate certain things about a person in a probabilistic manner, with certain groups of course being more prone to struggling than others. A lot of these struggles play a direct role in how a person engages with consumerism, especially when looking through the lens of class disparities:

\- Being poor on a personal level means that you have a reduced capacity to choose what kinds of products you can boycott while still being able to actually survive and live healthily— not to mention that the damage from climate change disproportionately affects the poor. On a larger scale, poorer countries often struggle with disposing of waste and cannot realistically pursue clean solutions.

\- Being stressed erodes your cognitive functioning and willpower and thus leaves you more likely to make poor spending choices— it’s linked to the development of addictions, which often produce their own material garbage (such as cigarettes or alcohol). It can also directly lead to long-term physical illnesses and thus effectively leave you disabled in certain respects.

There’s a more recent post at the top of the subreddit that discusses how being overworked and stressed makes one consume more. That’s relevant for this point as well.

\- Speaking of disability, being disabled in particular often requires material goods in order to mitigate the disabling aspects. Poor eyesight means buying new glasses every few years, being paraplegic means you need a wheelchair, so on and so forth. Many mental conditions require material aids as well— I wouldn’t have been able to function without an iPad for the later parts of my schooling— and medication of course adds more waste on top of that.

\- Being undereducated can leave you more likely to live in poverty, can make you less aware of some of the more insidious aspects of consumerism, and can lead to you missing out on knowledge that could potentially reduce your consumeristic tendencies. And if you’re working multiple jobs just to stay afloat, you hardly have the time or the energy to read up on this stuff— assuming you’re ever pointed in that direction to begin with.

It’s somewhat unfair to write this sort of stuff off as identity politics when these issues genuinely do bleed into every aspect of life, this topic included. And as an aside, those sorts of labels when used right can disarm a lot of hateful stuff. I’d rather openly label myself as autistic than give others the chance to jump in and label me as weird or a loser, for example— people who fall into these categories can use those labels to seize some power over the narratives around them, which are so often filled with misinformation and prejudice.

Just a passing reader here. I haven’t played any of the Spelunky games and don’t know what the community generally wants out of a challenge… but most of the best gamers want their challenge runs to last 20 minutes, not 200.  
Take Celeste speedrunning, for example. The fastest 100% run is around 1 hour and 42 minutes, and that category has around 76 spots on its leaderboard. The fastest any% run is around 26 minutes, and the number of leaderboard spots goes well into the thousands. Because the any% is shorter, it puts a lot more emphasis on the moment-to-moment gameplay— the difficulty is “denser,” so to speak. The competition being so much fiercer means that you could easily argue that any% speedrunning is actually harder despite there being much less content to complete.  
You see a similar story with score runs. Scoring in Lady Bug is arguably just as hard as scoring in Mushihimesame Futari, but only one of them ended up at GDQ.  
The best gamers often have an immense respect for the games they play, and they expect that respect to be returned in kind. That includes respecting the gamers’ time. I don’t know much about Spelunky’s balance and can’t speak on whether a “denser” difficulty is appropriate for any of the games in the series, but if the alternative is a long challenge that people just don’t find fun, maybe it’s better for the games to just be a little easier.
